description: Australia Awards Scholarships are long-term awards administered by the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade and funded by the Australian Government. They provide opportunities for people from developing countries, particularly those located in the Indo-Pacific region, to undertake full-time undergraduate or postgraduate study at participating Australian universities and Technical and Further Education (TAFE) institutions. Eligibility is limited to citizens of, and applicants residing in and applying from, the 59 countries and regions on the official participating countries list, and applicants apply through the OASIS online portal during a single annual window published by country. Award holders sign a contract with the Commonwealth of Australia and must leave Australia for a minimum of two years after completing the scholarship, failing which they may incur a debt to the Commonwealth for the total accrued cost of their Scholarship Benefit.

programme_duration.official_range: Policy Handbook 2.6.6: 'The maximum duration of study permitted for a Bachelor's degree is four years. Double Bachelor's degrees are permitted so long as both are included in the original offer and both can be completed within four years.' Preparation programs (2.6.21) 'can be up to a maximum of 12 months' and the total program of activities 'must not result in the scholarship duration being more than 12 months longer than the main course'. For comparison, the published maxima at other levels are two years for a Master's degree (2.6.10) and four years for a doctorate program (2.6.14). The award is made 'for the minimum period necessary for the individual to complete the academic program specified by the Australian higher education institution, including any preparatory training'.
programme_duration.renewal_note: The award is not renewed; it is granted once for the period needed to complete the institution-specified program, and all scholarships must be taken up in the year for which they are awarded (Policy Handbook 2.6.1). Changes to length are variations processed in OASIS under Chapter 13, including extensions (13.3), suspensions (13.4), transfers (13.5), upgrades (13.6) and reductions (13.7), and require approval from Program Areas and the Australia Awards Section rather than automatic continuation.

funding.scholarship_type: Competitive government development scholarship with a full entitlement package and a service/return obligation
funding.monthly_amount_note: No monthly amount is published. The official source publishes a daily rate, not a monthly one: Policy Handbook Table 1 states 'From 1 January 2026, the CLE rate is A$99.26 per day (or approximately A$36,230 per annum)', with the worked examples 'In a leap year the CLE for a scholarship will be: 366 * A$99.26 = A$36,329.16' and 'In a non-leap year, the CLE for a scholarship will be: 365 * A$99.26 = A$36,229.90'. The Contribution to Living Expenses is described as 'a fortnightly contribution to basic living expenses paid at a rate determined by the department'.
funding.travel_amount_note: No airfare value is published. The entitlement is defined in kind, not as a cash amount: Table 1 records 'Mobilisation travel — Booked and paid for by Program Areas on behalf of the scholar. Payment of a single economy class airfare to Australia from the home country via the most direct and economical route at the commencement of the scholarship' and 'Completion travel — Payment of a single economy class airfare from Australia to the home country via the most direct and economical route at the completion of the scholarship'.
funding.fully_funded_note: The package is extensive but is not unconditionally fully funded, for three reasons recorded in the official sources. First, Policy Handbook 1.1.4 and the official award page impose a two-year return obligation, and failure to comply 'may result in the scholar incurring a debt to the Commonwealth of Australia for the total accrued cost of their Scholarship Benefit', so the award carries a service bond. Second, 1.1.7 states 'The Australian Government does not provide any financial support for the dependents of scholars. Scholars are responsible, including financially, for their family members who accompany them to Australia.' Third, the entitlements that apply are qualified: OSHC covers basic medical costs only and excludes pre-existing conditions, the establishment allowance is 'a contribution' rather than a reimbursement of actual costs, pre-course English and supplementary academic support are conditional on assessment, fieldwork is for research purposes only, and the reunion airfare is available only to unaccompanied scholars.

tuition.conditions: Policy Handbook 1.1.5(i) lists 'full tuition fees'. Table 1 describes the item as 'Academic Fees — Paid by the Australia Awards Section directly to the institution. Covers the course costs and all compulsory academic fees that apply to international students.' A separate item, the Student Services and Amenities Fee, is also 'Paid by the Australia Awards Section directly to the institution' and 'Covers the fee payable to institutions for the provision of necessary student services.' No tuition figure is published.

monthly_stipend.conditions: Contribution to Living Expenses (CLE), also referred to as a Stipend: 'Paid by the Australia Awards Section to the institution to distribute to the scholar. A fortnightly Contribution to Living Expenses (CLE) paid at a rate determined by DFAT. From 1 January 2026, the CLE rate is A$99.26 per day (or approximately A$36,230 per annum).' No fortnightly or monthly figure is published, so amount is null.

travel_allowance.conditions: Mobilisation travel to Australia and completion travel home, each a single economy class airfare via the most direct and economical route, booked and paid by the Program Area on the scholar's behalf (Table 1, sections 10.7 and 10.9). Separately, a reunion airfare is available to unaccompanied scholars for return travel to their home country during institution semester breaks (section 10.8), and a fieldwork airfare is available for research purposes (section 12.3). No airfare value is published.

installation_allowance.conditions: Table 1: 'Establishment Allowance — Paid by the Australia Awards Section to the institution to distribute to the scholar. A contribution of A$5,000 towards expenses such as rental bonds, textbooks, study materials, additional medical insurance, home contents insurance etc. paid by the institution when the scholar arrives in Australia.' Section 10.2.2 adds 'study materials – including IT equipment, laboratory coats, additional medical insurance and home contents insurance' and states it is 'paid in a lump sum for scholars to use at their discretion'.

visa_support.conditions: Table 1: 'Visa expenses — Paid by Program Areas on behalf of the scholar. Payment of visa processing and medical checks necessary for gaining the Student visa (subclass 500).' Policy Handbook 1.1.5(vii) lists this as 'Initial visa expenses'. No dollar figure is published. Dependant visa costs are not covered.

insurance.conditions: Table 1: 'Overseas Student Health Cover (OSHC) — Paid by the Australia Awards Section to the institution to then arrange and pay for on behalf of the scholar. Single OSHC will be provided to cover the DFAT scholar's basic medical costs. Scholars may purchase, at their own expense, additional medical insurance to cover ancillary services such as dentist, optometrist, physiotherapist, etc.' The award page adds 'for the duration of the award (for award holder only) – provided to cover the scholar's basic medical costs (with the exception of pre-existing conditions)'. No dollar figure is published.

research_allowance.conditions: Fieldwork, available 'for research awards and Masters by coursework which have a research component where fieldwork is compulsory', provides 'one return economy class airfare via the most direct route to their country of citizenship or within Australia' (award page; Policy Handbook 1.1.6(iii) and section 12.3). Supplementary Academic Support (SAS) funds are separate: 'Institutions may expend these funds at a rate of A$500 every six months that the scholar is on-scholarship', accrued at A$500 every six months, i.e. A$1,000 a year (section 12.2.2). Neither is available to a bachelor's student by default; fieldwork is limited to research purposes and a compulsory research component.

book_allowance.conditions: No separate book allowance is published. Textbook and study-material costs are covered inside the A$5,000 establishment allowance, which is 'a contribution towards expenses such as rental bonds, textbooks, study materials, additional medical insurance, home contents insurance etc.' (Table 1). Supplementary Academic Support funds may also be expended by the institution on eligible educational services, at A$500 every six months.

equipment_allowance.conditions: No separate equipment allowance is published. Policy Handbook 10.2.2 lists 'study materials – including IT equipment, laboratory coats' among the expenses the A$5,000 establishment allowance contributes towards. Supplementary Academic Support may additionally fund eligible educational services at A$500 every six months.

family_allowance.note: Policy Handbook 1.1.7: 'The Australian Government does not provide any financial support for the dependents of scholars. Scholars are responsible, including financially, for their family members who accompany them to Australia.' The OASIS Applicant User Guide repeats this in Section 3. Dependant visa costs, travel and living costs are not covered.

accommodation_support.conditions: Financial support only; no accommodation is provided. The A$5,000 establishment allowance is 'a contribution towards expenses such as rental bonds', paid in a lump sum for the scholar to use at their discretion (Table 1 and section 10.2.2). Sections 11.3 and 10.7.2 describe arrival and accommodation arrangements as institutional support processes, not as funded housing.

bond.conditions: Applicants who accept the award sign a contract with the Commonwealth of Australia. The official award page states: 'Scholars are required to leave Australia for a minimum of two years after completing their scholarship. Failure to do so will result in the scholar incurring a debt for the total accrued cost of their scholarship.' Policy Handbook 1.1.4: 'Scholars are required to leave Australia and not apply for a visa to return for a minimum of two years after completing their scholarship. Failure to do so may result in the scholar incurring a debt to the Commonwealth of Australia for the total accrued cost of their Scholarship Benefit.' Scholarship condition 6.2.1(v) requires scholars to 'leave Australia for a minimum of two years within 30 days of their Scholarship End Date, or within 14 days of their scholarship termination or withdrawal date, or on the expiring of their student (subclass 500) visa, whichever occurs first'. Section 8.7.3 makes the exclusion period cumulative. Section 8.7.8 records that the payment of a debt is legally enforceable and that having a debt to the Commonwealth affects subsequent visa support.

total_estimated_value.note: No total award value is published in any official source, and the components are rate-based (A$99.26 per day CLE, A$5,000 establishment allowance, A$2,500 IAP contribution, A$500 per six months SAS) rather than a single headline figure. No total has been computed.

coverage_limitations: The award carries a service bond. Scholars must leave Australia for a minimum of two years after completing the scholarship, and failure to do so may result in a debt to the Commonwealth for the total accrued cost of their Scholarship Benefit, which is legally enforceable. The two-year exclusion period is cumulative, so time spent in Australia during the period may extend it.

The Australian Government provides no financial support for dependents: 'Scholars are responsible, including financially, for their family members who accompany them to Australia' (Policy Handbook 1.1.7). Dependant visa costs, travel and living costs are not covered.

OSHC is single cover for the scholar only and excludes pre-existing conditions. Ancillary services such as dentist, optometrist and physiotherapist require additional insurance purchased at the scholar's own expense.
The establishment allowance is a fixed A$5,000 contribution towards a list of start-up costs, not a reimbursement of actual accommodation or textbook costs.

The exact benefit structure may differ between scholars: the award page says the listed benefits 'generally apply', Policy Handbook 10.1.1 states 'The costs covered by the scholarship are detailed in each scholar's scholarship contract', and 10.1.3 states 'These costs are subject to change'.

Pre-course English, supplementary academic support, fieldwork and the reunion airfare are conditional, not universal. Pre-course English is capped at six months and is available only where the scholar is within half an IELTS point, 10 TOEFL points or 7 PTE points of the institution's requirement.

The reunion airfare is available only to unaccompanied scholars who remain unaccompanied in Australia for twelve months and are enrolled for a minimum of two academic years; a scholar who becomes accompanied at any point loses the entitlement permanently (10.8.3 and 10.8.5).
No monetary value for air travel, tuition or the fortnightly CLE instalment is published, so the cash worth of the package cannot be totalled from official sources.

Fieldwork is available only for research purposes and only for research awards and Masters by coursework with a compulsory research component; it is not available for a standard bachelor's degree by coursework.

Australia Awards Scholarships are not available for undergraduate courses that are available at tertiary education institutions in the scholar's home country (Policy Handbook 2.7.1(i)), so the eligible course range is narrower than the full Australian catalogue.

Country and regional profiles, not the global pages, govern what is actually available: priority fields of study, the level of course available, document certification requirements and local eligibility rules all vary, and Policy Handbook 2.6.5 notes that 'some Program Areas do not provide scholarships for undergraduate or PhD studies'.

final_year_condition: For the bachelor's track the entry qualification is completion of secondary school, not a bachelor's degree. The OASIS Applicant User Guide, Section 9 (Qualifications), instructs applicants: 'If you have not completed your studies, please list the expected completion date', so a qualification not yet completed may be recorded in the application. Admission is nevertheless assessed later: Policy Handbook 2.2.1(ix) requires the applicant to 'be able to satisfy the admission requirements of the institution at which the award is to be undertaken' and notes this 'may not be known until Program Areas request a placement at selected institutions', while 5.1.2 states that an institution will process a placement offer only where the scholar meets the institution's admission requirements. However, Policy Handbook 2.8.2(i)-(ii) requires 'a certified copy of original formal degree graduation certificate (i.e. testamur)' and certified official transcripts as application documents, so a final-year student who cannot yet produce a certified secondary-school certificate should confirm with their in-country Program Area whether a certificate of expected completion can substitute at the application stage.
equivalent_degree_note: Equivalent secondary-school qualifications from other countries are accepted. Admission and recognition are assessed by the Australian institution against the CRICOS-listed course: Policy Handbook 5.1.2 provides that institutions process a placement offer only where the scholar meets the institution's admission requirements, including English language requirements, and is assessed as capable of completing the nominated course within the period 'as recorded on the CRICOS website'. Section 5.1.1(vii) also covers 'recognition of credit received for prior study and course length, fees and entitlements adjusted accordingly where appropriate'. The official pages name no specific credential-evaluation body, so no equivalence framework is asserted.

age_limit.age_calculation_date: 1 February of the year of commencing the scholarship

nationality_quota: Scholarships are allocated by country and region against budget. Policy Handbook 4.3.1: the selection process in each country or region 'will result in a list of successful candidates equal to the number of scholarships available for the country or region'. 4.3.4: 'Scholarship numbers are determined by the budget available to fund them.' No per-country number or quota is published on any official page read.

eligibility.citizenship: Restricted to citizens of a participating country. The official participating countries page lists 59 countries and regions across three groupings: Africa (Algeria, Angola, Botswana, Cote d'Ivoire, Democratic Republic of Congo, Egypt, Ethiopia, The Gambia, Ghana, Guinea, Kenya, Madagascar, Malawi, Mauritius, Morocco, Mozambique, Namibia, Nigeria, Rwanda, Sierra Leone, South Africa, Tanzania, Uganda, Zambia and Zimbabwe); Asia (Bangladesh, Bhutan, Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Maldives, Mongolia, Myanmar, Nepal, Pakistan, Philippines, Singapore, Sri Lanka, Thailand and Vietnam); and the Pacific (Federated States of Micronesia, French Polynesia, Fiji, Kiribati, Naoero, New Caledonia, Niue, Palau, Papua New Guinea, Republic of the Marshall Islands, Samoa, Solomon Islands, Timor-Leste, Tonga, Tuvalu, Vanuatu and Wallis and Futuna). Policy Handbook 2.2.1(ii): applicants must 'be a citizen of a participating country (as listed on the Australia Awards website)'. Applicants must also be residing in and applying from a developing country that is eligible for Australia Awards Scholarships. 2.2.1(iii) excludes Australian citizens, Australian permanent residents and applicants for permanent residence.
eligibility.residence_requirement: Applicants must be residing in and applying from an eligible developing country (Policy Handbook 2.2.1(ii)). Three exceptions are listed in 2.2.2: applicants working for their government, a regional organisation or civil society in a third country; applicants studying in Australian or New Zealand secondary schools; and applicants residing in the immediate region to which an award would be willing to be granted, with the award reported as belonging to the applicant's country of citizenship. No minimum period of prior residence is published.

age_limit.age_calculation_date: 1 February of the year of commencing the scholarship

eligibility.secondary_school_requirement: For the bachelor's track the entry qualification is completion of secondary school, evidenced by a certified copy of the formal graduation certificate and official transcripts. Policy Handbook 2.8.2 requires a certified copy of the original formal degree graduation certificate and official academic transcripts, certified translations where not in English, and 2.8.7-2.8.9 set the certification standard. The OASIS Applicant User Guide Section 9 instructs applicants to list all qualifications, complete or incomplete, starting with the highest, and to give an expected completion date where studies are not finished.
eligibility.academic_requirements: There is no published minimum grade point average or percentage. Eligibility is defined as being able to satisfy the admission requirements of the institution at which the award is to be undertaken (2.2.1(ix)), assessed at placement, and the proposed course must be in a priority development sector for the applicant's country and must not be at an academic level lower than one already achieved (OASIS Applicant User Guide, Section 8). Policy Handbook 4.1.1 states 'All applications for Australia Awards are considered on merit providing equal opportunity to all applicants.'
eligibility.language_requirement: Mandatory. Policy Handbook 2.4.4: 'English language scores are not negotiable. All Australia Awards Scholarship scholars must meet the following requirement: an Academic IELTS result with an overall score of at least 6.5, with no band less than 6.0, or an internet based TOEFL score of at least 4.5 (on the new scale dated 21 January 2026) or 84 (on the old scale applying prior to 21 January 2026), with a minimum of 21 in all subtests, or PTE Academic overall score of 58 with no communicative skill score less than 50.' Applicants meet DFAT's requirement without a test only where 'their first language is English and if they have undertaken their education in English (evidenced by their academic transcripts)' (2.4.1). Where an institution's requirement is higher than DFAT's, the institution's applies (2.4.5).
eligibility.work_experience: Not a published universal requirement. Work and voluntary experience are recorded in OASIS Sections 12 and 13, and the OASIS Applicant User Guide notes that 'Current employment may include work experience and voluntary work'. Policy Handbook 2.2.1(viii) allows Program Areas or home governments to add specific criteria, 'e.g. having worked a certain number of years in an appropriate sector', so a work-experience requirement may apply in individual countries but is not universal. Academic referee reports are required regardless.
eligibility.extracurricular_requirement: Not a published universal requirement. Professional memberships are recorded in OASIS Section 15 and may include 'community, cultural, political, scientific, professional or educational organisations'. Selection does consider 'the applicant's professional and personal qualities' (4.1.4), and the OASIS supporting statement and referee reports provide the vehicle for demonstrating them.
eligibility.leadership_requirement: Leadership potential is the central published selection criterion. Policy Handbook 4.1.4: 'Selection of applicants will consider the applicant's professional and personal qualities, academic competence and, most importantly, their potential to impact on development challenges in their home country.' The highest scoring band, 'Outstanding: greater than or equal to 90%', is defined as 'an outstanding candidate with strong academic capacity and demonstrated leadership capacities in strategic and inspirational thinking and practice, who is very likely to make a significant impact in their field of practice in home country and internationally'.
eligibility.financial_need: Not a published selection criterion. No income test, means test or financial-need assessment appears in the Policy Handbook eligibility criteria, the selection criteria or the OASIS application. The award is a merit-based development award, not a needs-based one.
eligibility.previous_scholarship_restriction: Applicants must not have previously received a long-term Australia Award in the previous four years (2.2.1(vi)) and must not be receiving or have accepted an offer of any other scholarship, sponsorship or financial award that duplicates or overlaps Australia Awards Scholarship entitlements (2.2.1(xiii)). All current or previous scholarships or financial support must be disclosed as part of the application. Recording other scholarship applications in OASIS is not itself disqualifying (OASIS Applicant User Guide, Sections 6 and 7: 'Applying for more than one scholarship does not make you ineligible to apply for an Australia Awards Scholarship' and 'Entering this information will not have any effect on the outcome of your Australia Awards Scholarships application'). The June 2026 Policy Handbook change log records that the rules on concurrent financial support were strengthened 'to prevent duplicate funding, reinforce fraud controls', and that 'Section 13.7 provides clearer, more explicit rules around concurrent or overlapping financial support'. Undisclosed relevant information, including returning home without DFAT or institutional approval, is treated as fraudulent under the fraud management framework in Chapter 3, and monetary fraud or misuse of entitlements may lead to suspension during investigation and termination where substantiated.
eligibility.enrolment_status_requirement: Applicants are not required to hold an offer of place at an Australian institution when they apply. Policy Handbook 2.5.1: 'Scholarship applicants are not required to have an offer of place at an Australian institution when they apply. However, applicants must have researched their preferred courses... and ensure that it is included on the CRICOS Register.' The official FAQ answers 'Do I need to contact universities directly?' with 'No. Applicants do not need to contact Australian universities when applying for an Australia Awards Scholarship.' Placement is requested through OASIS by the Program Area after selection (5.1.1). Australia Awards Scholarships do not support completion of studies already commenced in Australia (2.6.3) or study for a lesser degree than one already held (2.6.4 and 2.7.2).
eligibility.health_requirement: All applicants and scholars must meet the Department of Home Affairs requirements to hold a Student visa (subclass 500), which includes health examinations. Program Areas arrange health checks, and 'Payment of visa processing and medical checks necessary for gaining the Student visa (subclass 500)' is a scholarship entitlement (Policy Handbook Table 1). Section 8.3 covers visa requirements for scholars with disability and Chapter 9 sets out disability-inclusive support. Policy Handbook 2.1.1 warns that pre-existing conditions may be aggravated by the stress of the scholarship and that applicants should research Australian conditions before applying, and OSHC excludes pre-existing conditions. No general medical fitness certificate is required at application.
eligibility.field_restrictions: The proposed course must be in a priority development sector for the applicant's country as listed on the participating country profile. Australia Awards Scholarships are not available for: undergraduate courses that are available at tertiary education institutions in the scholar's home country; training in areas related to nuclear technology or flying aircraft (the official FAQ notes Aviation Management is available); legal workshops; study by distance, online or external mode other than as part of a CRICOS-registered course where most units are undertaken in person and the external component is no more than one third of the total course study load; military training; and training in counter-subversion methods, the suppression of political dissent or intelligence procurement (2.7.1). DFAT reserves the right to exclude additional programs case by case (2.7.3). At least two-thirds of the course must be delivered in person, with at least one in-person unit every study period (2.5.4).

academic_requirements.percentage_note: No minimum percentage, grade point average or class of degree is published anywhere in the Policy Handbook, the OASIS Applicant User Guide or the official web pages. The academic test is the admission requirements of the host institution (2.2.1(ix)) and the merit-based selection described in 4.1, not a numerical academic threshold. The only percentages published relate to selection scoring bands, which are a guide to how Program Areas might score an application and are not an entry threshold.
academic_requirements.programme_specific_requirements: The proposed course must be listed on CRICOS and must be in a priority development sector for the applicant's country as published on the participating country profile (OASIS Applicant User Guide, Section 8). The type and level of course available varies by country: Policy Handbook 2.6.5 requires applicants to read the relevant Country or Regional Profile because 'some Program Areas do not provide scholarships for undergraduate or PhD studies'. The applicant must not be applying for a course at an academic level lower than one already achieved (2.2.1(xi), 2.6.4, 2.7.2). At least two-thirds of the course must be delivered in person with at least one in-person unit in every study period (2.5.4).
selection_factors_may_include: Potential to impact on development challenges in the home country, described in 4.1.4 as 'most importantly' (4.1.4)
Contribution of the proposed study program to building leadership in support of the home country's development (4.1.5 scoring table)
Demonstrated leadership capacities in strategic and inspirational thinking and practice (4.1.5 scoring table)
Likelihood of significant impact in the candidate's field of practice in the home country and internationally (4.1.5 scoring table)
Ability to develop networks while in Australia and promote Australia in the home country after completion (4.1.6)
Match with the desired profile and the development strategy areas being targeted (4.1.6)
Quality of the reintegration plan, which applicants must propose as part of their application (4.2.1 and 4.2.2)
Performance at interview, since the selection process must include an interview of shortlisted candidates (4.1.3)
academic_requirements.holistic_selection_note: Selection is a country- or region-level competitive process run by DFAT Program Areas, not a formula. Policy Handbook 4.1.1 states that 'All applications for Australia Awards are considered on merit providing equal opportunity to all applicants' and 4.1.2 that 'Program Areas manage the selection process in each country/region and the selection process is detailed in the relevant Country or Region Profile'. 4.1.3 requires an interview of shortlisted candidates and Australian Government representation on all interview panels. 4.1.5 publishes a non-binding five-band scoring guide (Outstanding at 90% and above, Very good 80-89%, Good 70-79%, Satisfactory 60-69%, Limited below 60%) that the handbook describes as 'a guide for applicants to understand how Program Areas might score an applicant'. Applications are not assessed on a rolling basis and are all reviewed after the closing date (official FAQ).

english_requirement.minimum_ielts: Academic IELTS overall score of at least 6.5, with no band less than 6.0
english_requirement.minimum_toefl: TOEFL iBT score of at least 4.5 on the new scale dated 21 January 2026, or 84 on the old scale applying prior to 21 January 2026, with a minimum of 21 in all subtests
english_requirement.minimum_pte: PTE Academic overall score of 58, with no communicative skill score less than 50
english_requirement.moi_rule: Applicants meet DFAT's English language requirement without a test where 'their first language is English and if they have undertaken their education in English (evidenced by their academic transcripts)' (Policy Handbook 2.4.1). Both conditions must be satisfied. The handbook notes at 2.4.2 that 'some institutions may still require evidence of English language proficiency', and at 2.4.5 that where an institution's requirement is higher than DFAT's the scholar must meet the institution's requirement.
english_requirement.test_score_note: Policy Handbook 2.4.4: 'English language scores are not negotiable. All Australia Awards Scholarship scholars must meet the following requirement: an Academic IELTS result with an overall score of at least 6.5, with no band less than 6.0, or an internet based TOEFL score of at least 4.5 (on the new scale dated 21 January 2026) or 84 (on the old scale applying prior to 21 January 2026), with a minimum of 21 in all subtests, or PTE Academic overall score of 58 with no communicative skill score less than 50.' 2.4.4 also provides that only where an applicant does not satisfy the medium-of-instruction route 'the scholar ... provide an academic English language test result that meets the institution's academic English language requirement tests before commencing the approved main course of studies'. The June 2026 handbook change log records that the TOEFL entry was amended 'to account for the introduction of the new scoring scale from 21 January 2026 and ensures both new and legacy scores are recognised during the transition period'. TEST VALIDITY (2.4.3): 'Scholars' English language test results must be valid at 1 January of the year in which the scholar is commencing studies in Australia (IELTS, TOEFL scores, and PTE Academic are valid for two years after the test date). If an institution requires a different test validity timeframe, scholars must meet the institution's requirements.' 2.8.2(vii) gives the worked example: 'as results are normally valid for two years, the test date would need to have been taken after 1 January 2025 for an application for a scholarship to commence studies in 2027'. PRE-COURSE ENGLISH THRESHOLDS (2.4.6 and 2.4.7): country programs or institutions may provide in-country or in-Australia pre-course English, for a maximum of six months, where the scholar is within half a point of the required IELTS, within 10 points of the internet-based TOEFL, or within 7 points of the PTE Academic score of the institution's minimum requirement; 2.4.12 provides that 'An institution must not accept a scholar if they are unlikely to reach the standard of English required for the main course of studies within six months of PCE training.'

language_of_instruction.language_note: The language of instruction is English: all applicants 'should be prepared to undertake study in English' (Policy Handbook 2.1.1) and must meet the English language requirements in 2.4. Where a scholar does not meet them, the official sources fund pre-course English rather than an alternative-language pathway. The official pages do not enumerate the languages in which individual CRICOS-listed courses are taught, so no list of programme-specific languages is recorded.

application_method.application_route: Applicants apply directly, in most countries through the OASIS (Online Australia Awards Scholarships Information System) portal at https://oasis.dfat.gov.au, selecting the scheme 'Australia Awards Scholarships'. The official FAQ states 'Applications are submitted online through OASIS' and 'Applicants from Indonesia and the Philippines must apply through their country-specific portals: Australia Awards Indonesia; Australia Awards Philippines'. Where online application is not possible, a hard-copy route exists: the official How to apply page states 'Some countries encourage and allow you to apply online while others require hard-copy applications. See your participating country profile for more information' and 'If you are unable to submit your application online, you can apply by mail. Please check your participating country profile for contact details to obtain a hardcopy application form and any other templates such as referee reports (if applicable).' Completed hard-copy applications and supporting documentation must be submitted by the deadline specified for the country. No university nomination or agent nomination is required, and applicants do not contact universities for admission.
application_steps: Check that your country is on the official participating countries list and read your country profile for priority fields of study, eligible course levels, document certification requirements and local eligibility rules
Read the Australia Awards Scholarships Policy Handbook in full before applying, as required by the official How to apply page
Check the opening and closing dates page and wait for the round to open for your country
Register in OASIS at https://oasis.dfat.gov.au; a unique registration number, username and temporary password are issued by email and a new one-time password is required at every logon
Create a new application and select 'Australia Awards Scholarships' from the scheme drop-down; the intake defaults to the current round

Complete all 18 sections of the application: personal details, contact details, spouse details, children details, emergency contact details, previous scholarships, scholarship applications, proposed study program, qualifications, English language details, computer literacy details, current employment, previous employment, supporting statement, professional memberships, communication, documentary evidence and declaration

Add two course preferences in the Proposed Study Program section, entering the seven-digit CRICOS course code and selecting the institution, and indicate whether each is your first, second or third preference

Upload all required documentary evidence on the Documentary Evidence screen; each document is limited to 2MB and only .doc, .docx, rtf, .pdf, .gif, .jpeg, .jpg, .tiff, .png, .bmp and .txt are accepted
Tick the Declaration and Acknowledgement screen and press Submit; every section of the checklist must show as complete before submission is possible
Before the closing date, edit freely as a draft, or un-submit and resubmit an amended application; after the closing date the application cannot be edited or resubmitted
If shortlisted, attend an interview and supply any further documentation requested
If selected, sign the scholarship agreement with the Commonwealth of Australia after a placement offer is received from an Australian institution
application_method.application_fee: No application fee is mentioned in any official source read: the Australia Awards Scholarships page, the How to apply page, the FAQ, the Australia Awards Scholarships Policy Handbook (June 2026) and the OASIS Applicant User Guide (January 2026) all publish no fee for applying. No fee should be inferred from this absence, but none is recorded.

official_application_documents.document_language: Documents must be in English, or accompanied by a certified translation into English. official_application_documents.document_format: Uploaded through OASIS. The official FAQ and the OASIS Applicant User Guide state: 'There is a 2MB limit per document uploaded. OASIS will accept only the following documents types: .doc, .docx, rtf, .pdf, .gif, .jpeg, .jpg, .tiff, .png, .bmp, .txt.' Documents are uploaded by selecting the +Add icon on the Documentary Evidence screen, choosing the document type, adding a description and saving, after which all uploaded documents appear as a list on that screen. For the bachelor's track the degree certificate and transcripts are secondary-school documents, and 2.8.2(i)-(ii) refers to them as 'a certified copy of original formal degree graduation certificate (i.e. testamur)' and 'a certified copy of original formal academic transcript/s', with the certification standard in 2.8.7-2.8.9 applying to them. OASIS Section 9 separately records every academic qualification, complete or incomplete, by level of study starting with the highest, entered one at a time, with an expected completion date where studies are not finished.
official_application_documents.transcript_requirement: Mandatory and certified: 'a certified copy of original formal academic transcript/s and, if not in English, a certified translation copy of the transcript/s' (Policy Handbook 2.8.2(ii)).
official_application_documents.certified_translation_requirement: Certified, not merely literal. Every document not in English requires a certified translation (2.8.2). For the bachelor's track the degree certificate and transcripts are secondary-school documents, and 2.8.2(i)-(ii) refers to them as 'a certified copy of original formal degree graduation certificate (i.e. testamur)' and 'a certified copy of original formal academic transcript/s'. The certification standard is set by 2.8.8-2.8.9: the original must have been sighted and the copy sworn to be a true copy by an authorised person at the official records department of the issuing institution, an Australian overseas diplomatic mission, or a Notary Public; the authorised person must write 'This is a certified true copy of the original document as sighted by me', sign and print name, address, contact telephone number, profession or occupation or organisation and the date verified, and include the official stamp or seal of the verifier's organisation if it has one (2.8.9). Where an institution has additional certification requirements, the scholar must meet the institution's requirements (2.8.10).

The official FAQ states 'Country Profiles outline: Priority fields of study, Eligible institutions and courses, Document certification requirements, Local eligibility rules.' selection_process.decision_maker: DFAT Program Areas manage the selection process in each country or region, with the process set out in the relevant Country or Region Profile (Policy Handbook 4.1.2). The Australian Government must be represented on all interview panels, and the selection committee must be chaired by a DFAT officer at the APS 6 or EL1 level, or by a Counsellor, and may include a representative from a country or regional desk (4.1.3). The Australia Awards Section provides on-demand assistance to Program Areas and further guidance on undertaking the selection process is available in the document section of OASIS.
selection_process.selection_type: Competitive in-country or in-region selection after a single annual closing date: eligibility check, shortlisting, mandatory interview of shortlisted candidates, panel scoring against country criteria, and a ranked list of successful and reserve candidates

Interview of shortlisted candidates, which may also include other activities such as group participation sessions to assess suitability (4.1.3)
Selection panel scores the application and ranks candidates

Institution assesses the request on merit and issues a placement offer where the scholar meets admission and English requirements and is assessed as capable of completing the course within the CRICOS period (5.1.2)

selection_process.weighting_note: No numerical weighting is published for any criterion. 4.1.4 states only that selection 'will consider the applicant's professional and personal qualities, academic competence and, most importantly, their potential to impact on development challenges in their home country', and that 'Each country or region may have additional selection criteria'. 4.1.5 publishes a five-band scoring guide (Outstanding at 90% and above, Very good 80-89%, Good 70-79%, Satisfactory 60-69%, Limited below 60%) explicitly described as 'a guide for applicants to understand how Program Areas might score an applicant', not as a weighting scheme. HOW THE PUBLISHED CRITERIA ARE APPLIED: academic competence is one of the three named considerations in 4.1.4 and 'strong academic capacity' appears in the Outstanding band of the 4.1.5 table, but there is no published minimum grade, with academic standing tested through the host institution's admission requirements at placement (2.2.1(ix) and 5.1.2); leadership is the dominant criterion, since the 4.1.5 bands at every level are defined in terms of 'building leadership in support of home country's development' and 'demonstrated leadership capacities in strategic and inspirational thinking and practice', and 4.1.6 adds that applicants who demonstrate a significant ability to develop networks while in Australia and promote Australia in their home country 'will be favourably considered'; community service is framed as development contribution, with the bands assessing the study program's 'contribution to building leadership in support of home country's development' and 4.2 requiring a reintegration plan; extracurricular achievement is assessed indirectly through 'the applicant's professional and personal qualities' (4.1.4), the OASIS supporting statement, professional memberships (OASIS Section 15, which may include 'community, cultural, political, scientific, professional or educational organisations') and employment history including community and voluntary work (OASIS Sections 12 and 13); financial need is not a criterion at all, and no income test, means test or financial-need assessment appears in the eligibility criteria, the selection criteria or the OASIS application. No portfolio is required at any stage: the documentary requirement is the certified academic, identity and language document set plus referee reports, a CV and the OASIS supporting statement, with research applicants additionally supplying evidence of past research undertaken and its outcomes (2.6.13).
selection_process.results_timing: Selection outcomes are advised on completion of the process, 'generally August' (Policy Handbook 4.3.2 and 4.4.1). The official FAQ adds that 'Shortlisted candidates will be notified by mid-August 2026' and that 'Only successful applicants will be contacted directly'. Program Areas are not required to provide direct feedback to unsuccessful applicants, 'given the volume of applications' (4.4.1). The interview is mandatory for shortlisted candidates, not merely possible: 4.1.3 states 'The selection process must include an interview of short-listed candidates (approved by a senior DFAT officer at First Secretary level or above) and may include other activities such as group participation sessions to assess the suitability of applicants', the Australia Awards Scholarship Cycle summary likewise records that short-listed applicants are interviewed, and the official FAQ confirms that applications are assessed only after the closing date and that 'Only shortlisted candidates will be contacted for further steps, such as interviews or additional documentation'.
selection_process.scholarship_rank_note: Selection produces a ranked list. 4.3.1: the process 'will result in a list of successful candidates equal to the number of scholarships available for the country or region, and in most instances a list of reserve candidates ranked in order'. 4.3.4: reserve candidates are selected from high-quality unsuccessful applicants who meet all eligibility criteria and are deemed suitable for placement, where the opportunity arises, because 'Scholarship numbers are determined by the budget available to fund them.'

degree_outcome.awarded_qualification: A CRICOS-registered qualification from a participating Australian university or Technical and Further Education (TAFE) institution. For the bachelor's track this is a Bachelor's degree; the Handbook also permits a foundation program of up to 12 months before it (5.2.4) and an Honours year recommended by the institution for an outstanding scholar (2.6.7-2.6.9).
degree_outcome.typical_programme_length: Up to four years for a Bachelor's degree, being the maximum duration permitted under Policy Handbook 2.6.6; a double Bachelor's degree is permitted only if both are in the original offer and both can be completed within four years. The award itself is made 'for the minimum period necessary for the individual to complete the academic program specified by the Australian higher education institution, including any preparatory training', with preparation programs of up to 12 months and a total program no more than 12 months longer than the main course (2.6.21).
possible_awards: Double Bachelor's degree, within the four-year maximum
Bachelor's degree with Honours year, on institutional recommendation and Program Area approval

Articulated program combining a lower and a higher-level course, such as a vocational course articulating to an undergraduate degree, within two courses and the higher qualification's maximum duration
degree_outcome.degree_note: The scholarship does not confer a qualification itself; it funds a CRICOS-listed course at a participating Australian institution. The institution issues the qualification. Australia Awards Scholarships are only available for courses listed on CRICOS, and applicants need not have an offer of place when they apply, though they must research preferred courses and ensure they are on the Register (2.5.1). Scholarships must be taken up in the year for which they are awarded; should a scholar not commence by November in the year of the award, the offer is withdrawn and the applicant may reapply for the next intake (2.6.1).
degree_outcome.credit_transfer: Recognition of credit for prior study is handled by the institution and is reflected in the placement offer: Policy Handbook 5.1.1(vii) lists 'recognition of credit received for prior study and course length, fees and entitlements adjusted accordingly where appropriate' as part of what the placement offer specifies. No credit-transfer framework or minimum recognition rule is published.

student_rights_and_cost_protection.tuition_fee_for_recipients: Full tuition fees are covered. Policy Handbook 1.1.5(i) lists 'full tuition fees' and Table 1 records 'Academic Fees — Paid by the Australia Awards Section directly to the institution. Covers the course costs and all compulsory academic fees that apply to international students.' The Student Services and Amenities Fee is also paid directly to the institution.
student_rights_and_cost_protection.application_fee_for_recipients: No application fee is published in any official source read. The award page, How to apply page, FAQ, Policy Handbook and OASIS Applicant User Guide are all silent on any fee for applying.
student_rights_and_cost_protection.student_agreement: Yes. The official award page states: 'Applicants who want to accept an Australia Awards Scholarship will need to sign a contract with the Commonwealth of Australia declaring that they will comply with the conditions of the scholarship.' Policy Handbook 1.2.8 describes the handbook as underpinning the contract 'between DFAT and institutions to provide education services, and ... between the scholar and the Australian Government'. Successful candidates become scholars 'once the candidate has signed the scholarship agreement with the Commonwealth of Australia after a placement offer has been received from an Australian tertiary institution' (4.3.3). The contract's Schedule 1 sets out the Scholarship Benefit.
student_rights_and_cost_protection.common_services: Support is provided through the institution's Student Contact Officer, described at 1.3 and 11.1 as the officer designated by the institution to provide support services to Australia Awards Scholarship scholars, and as the first point of contact for scholars dealing with DFAT (scholarship condition 6.2.1(ix)). Institutions assist scholars to settle on arrival, provide the compulsory Introductory Academic Program (up to 6 weeks) and assist with subject selection (Australia Awards Scholarship Cycle, Arrival and Enrolment). Chapter 9 provides disability-inclusive support including reasonable adjustments and reasonable accommodations funded by DFAT under a Disability Support Agreement, assistive devices and mobility equipment, and Disability Support Persons. Chapter 14 governs welfare incidents, Chapter 15 critical incidents, and Chapter 16 natural disasters. DFAT Program Areas arrange pre-departure briefings (7.1) and reintegration assistance, and provide access to the Australia Awards Alumni Network (Chapter 18). Supplementary academic support is available through SAS funds at A$500 every six months.
student_rights_and_cost_protection.bond_requirement: Yes. Scholars are required to leave Australia for a minimum of two years after completing their scholarship, under a contract with the Commonwealth of Australia. Policy Handbook 1.1.4: 'Scholars are required to leave Australia and not apply for a visa to return for a minimum of two years after completing their scholarship.' Scholarship condition 6.2.1(v) requires leaving Australia 'for a minimum of two years within 30 days of their Scholarship End Date, or within 14 days of their scholarship termination or withdrawal date, or on the expiring of their student (subclass 500) visa, whichever occurs first'. Section 8.7.3(i) restates that scholars 'must not apply for a subsequent visa to return to Australia for a minimum of two years following their return home on completion of, termination of, or withdrawal from, the scholarship', and 8.7.3(ii) makes the period cumulative. All recipients and their dependants must hold subclass 500 visas for their time in Australia, with visa conditions that support the obligation to depart and remain outside Australia for at least two years (Chapter 8).
student_rights_and_cost_protection.bond_breach_consequence: The official award page states: 'Failure to do so will result in the scholar incurring a debt for the total accrued cost of their scholarship.' Policy Handbook 1.1.4 states the same in qualified terms: 'Failure to do so may result in the scholar incurring a debt to the Commonwealth of Australia for the total accrued cost of their Scholarship Benefit.' 8.7.8(iii) records that 'The payment of a debt is legally enforceable, payment does not entitle a scholar to DFAT's support for a subsequent visa and having a debt to the Commonwealth' counts against subsequent applications. 13.2.4 provides that scholars who withdraw after arriving in Australia and do not return home 'will be in breach of the requirements of the scholarship and may incur a debt to the Commonwealth for the scholarship costs'. 13.8 provides that if scholars do not depart Australia within 14 days after their scholarship is terminated, 'they will incur a debt to the Commonwealth for the total accrued cost of their scholarship'. Section 8.7.4 sets out the only circumstances in which DFAT may issue a Letter of No Objection supporting a subsequent visa, and 8.7.7 lists the cases in which it will not, including further study or research in Australia, a relationship or marriage to an Australian resident or citizen, dependants seeking to stay for schooling, study or work, and secured employment in Australia. The June 2026 handbook change log records that 1.1.4 was amended to align with 'a breach-based approach' and 'clearer discretion around application of debt and short-term travel provisions'.

programme_comparison_fields: The award is restricted to citizens of 59 participating countries, mostly in Africa, Asia and the Pacific; there is no open worldwide intake
It is one of the few fully packaged government awards: tuition, return air travel, establishment allowance, living expenses, health cover and visa costs are all covered
The published rates are unusually specific: A$99.26 per day CLE from 1 January 2026, A$5,000 establishment allowance, A$2,500 IAP contribution and A$500 per six months SAS
The two-year return obligation with an enforceable debt for the total accrued cost of the Scholarship Benefit is a materially harder condition than a typical home-country return expectation
There is no financial-need test, unlike needs-based university awards
Selection is run in-country by DFAT Program Areas with a mandatory interview, not centrally by DFAT or by a university
The application is a single annual window with a hard close; OASIS shuts at 14:00 AEST and there is no exception
Applications are not assessed on a rolling basis, so submitting early confers no advantage
Applicants do not need an offer of place and must not contact universities for admission; placement is arranged through OASIS after selection
Two course preferences are mandatory, and course preferences cannot be changed after submission (Policy Handbook 2.5.1)
Indonesia and the Philippines do not use OASIS and apply through country-specific portals
The reunion airfare exists only for unaccompanied scholars, which is unusual among comparable awards
practical_application_data.motivation_letter_strategy: There is no standalone motivation letter; the argument is made through the OASIS supporting statement (Section 14) and the reintegration plan, both read by the selection panel at shortlisting and at decision. The supporting statement fields are capped at 2,000 characters each and characters beyond the limit are not shown to the panel, so draft tightly and count. Build the response around the three factors named in Policy Handbook 4.1.4: professional and personal qualities, academic competence, and above all potential to impact on development challenges in the home country. Tie the proposed course explicitly to the priority development sector published in your country profile, because the official FAQ states 'Study programs must relate to your country's priority areas for development'. Make the reintegration plan concrete and practical, as 4.2.2 requires 'practical and realistic examples of tasks on which they plan to apply the skills and knowledge gained through their studies in Australia' together with 'the possible constraints they think could prevent them from achieving these tasks and mitigation strategies to overcome challenges'. Use the CV and referee reports to corroborate leadership and development-relevant experience rather than to repeat the statement. Note the official rule on artificial intelligence: 'Applicants may only use AI for basic tasks like spelling, grammar and organising ideas. AI must not be used to write, improve or paraphrase any part of your application. All responses must be your own original work. Misuse may result in disqualification.'

risk_flags.impact: Applicants from non-participating countries, and applicants who cannot apply from their country of citizenship, are ineligible regardless of merit. risk_flags.risk: Document certification is a common and hard-to-fix failure point

database_notes: SCOPE DETERMINATION - IN SCOPE, NO SUBSTITUTION MADE. This record is for Australia Awards Scholarships as directed, not a substituted award. RESEARCH_PROTOCOL permits records for scholarships hosted in an allowed region (Europe, US/America, Canada, Australia, Singapore, Malaysia). Host region here is Australia, an allowed region, and the scholarship is physically hosted and studied in Australia. The degree level is bachelor's, which is the level in scope. Because eligibility is restricted to nationals of specific countries, the protocol's second condition also has to be satisfied: eligibility must not be region-locked to a single excluded region. It is not. The official participating countries page lists 59 countries and regions spread across Africa, Asia and the Pacific, so no single excluded nationality is a gate on the award, and nationals of two allowed-region countries, Singapore and Malaysia, are eligible. The protocol's own carve-out that allows South-East Asian countries 'if the scholarship is physically hosted in an allowed region' also applies directly, since the award is hosted in Australia. Australia Awards Scholarships is therefore recorded as directed and no alternative award was substituted.

SOURCE ACCESS. Ten official-source fetches were made, all from dfat.gov.au subdomains: the award page, the Policy Handbook (June 2026), the OASIS Applicant User Guide (version 6.0, January 2026), the opening and closing dates page, the participating countries page, the How to apply page, the FAQ, the Australia Awards resources page, the two publication landing pages that carry the PDF links, and the participating institutions page. The OASIS portal itself was checked and returns HTTP 200. The live www.dfat.gov.au site was reachable only through a headless browser from this environment; the Policy Handbook and OASIS guide PDFs were retrieved and read in full text form from their official URLs, and every quotation in this record is taken verbatim from those official texts.

PARTICIPATING REGIONS INSIDE THE ALLOWED SCOPE (2 of 59 listed countries and regions): Singapore and Malaysia. Both are Asian countries named in the protocol's allowed host-region list, and nationals of both are eligible for Australia Awards Scholarships.

PARTICIPATING REGIONS OUTSIDE THE ALLOWED SCOPE (57 of 59 listed countries and regions), noted here and not used to bring the record into scope: Africa (25) Algeria, Angola, Botswana, Cote d'Ivoire, Democratic Republic of Congo, Egypt, Ethiopia, The Gambia, Ghana, Guinea, Kenya, Madagascar, Malawi, Mauritius, Morocco, Mozambique, Namibia, Nigeria, Rwanda, Sierra Leone, South Africa, Tanzania, Uganda, Zambia and Zimbabwe; South-East Asia other than Singapore and Malaysia (8) Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Myanmar, the Philippines, Thailand, Timor-Leste and Vietnam, plus Brunei; South Asia (6) Bangladesh, Bhutan, the Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka; East Asia (1) Mongolia; and Oceania other than Australia and New Zealand (17) Federated States of Micronesia, French Polynesia, Fiji, Kiribati, Naoero, New Caledonia, Niue, Palau, Papua New Guinea, Republic of the Marshall Islands, Samoa, Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu, Vanuatu and Wallis and Futuna. These are excluded for research-scope purposes only; the award itself remains recordable because its host region is allowed and its eligibility is not locked to any one of them.

DOCUMENT HIERARCHY. The most authoritative programmatic document for this record is the Australia Awards Scholarships Policy Handbook, updated June 2026, which sets out the aims, eligibility, benefits, selection, placement, financial entitlements, visa rules and the two-year exclusion. The OASIS Applicant User Guide, version 6.0, updated January 2026 and titled 'OASIS 2027 Intake', is the authoritative applicant-facing operational document and confirms the intake window, the two mandatory course preferences, the 18-section application, the 2MB and file-type limits and the closing rule. The official How to apply page explicitly requires applicants to read the Policy Handbook before applying, which is the basis for relying on it as the operating guide.

WHERE TO WATCH FOR UPDATES. The opening and closing dates page (https://www.dfat.gov.au/people-to-people/australia-awards/australia-awards-scholarships-opening-and-closing-dates) is the authoritative place to watch for the next round, because DFAT publishes each annual round's opening and closing times there. The Australia Awards resources page (https://www.dfat.gov.au/people-to-people/australia-awards/australia-awards-resources) is the secondary place, holding the current versions of the Policy Handbook, the Pacific Scholarships Handbook, the OASIS guide, the Australia Awards Scholarship Cycle, the AAS: New Applicant Journey Tracker and a useful links page, so it is where document updates appear. The Australia Awards Pacific Scholarships Policy Handbook (updated June 2023) held on that page is a separate document for a separate award hosted in the Pacific region and is not the operating guide for this record.

BENEFIT LIST - TWO OFFICIAL SOURCES DIFFER. The dfat.gov.au award page lists the general cover as full tuition fees, return air travel, establishment allowance, Contribution to Living Expenses, Introductory Academic Program, Overseas Student Health Cover, pre-course English fees, supplementary academic support and fieldwork. The Policy Handbook, at 1.1.5 and 1.1.6, additionally lists initial visa expenses and the reunion airfare, and separates the practices that vary between scholars. This record follows the Policy Handbook as the fuller and more authoritative list, and coverage_limitations records that the award page itself says the benefits 'generally apply' and differ between scholars, with Policy Handbook 10.1.1 stating the costs covered are detailed in each scholar's scholarship contract.

PECULIARITY OF THE PUBLISHED DATES. The official opening and closing dates page, the FAQ and the OASIS guide all express the opening time in AEDT (Australian Eastern Daylight Time, UTC+11) and the closing time in AEST (Australian Eastern Standard Time, UTC+10). This is not an inconsistency in the sources; Australian daylight saving ends in early April 2026, between the opening and the closing. The deadline time zone recorded in this file is AEST, matching the published closing time.

COUNTRY EXCEPTION TO THE SINGLE WINDOW. The official opening and closing dates page publishes one table headed 'Dates for study commencing in 2027', giving 1 February 2026 09:00 AEDT to 30 April 2026 14:00 AEST for all participating countries except Palau, for which it gives 30 March 2026 09:00 AEDT to 30 June 2026 14:00 AEST. application_deadline.single_central_deadline is true because a single central window governs the programme, with this one country exception recorded in application_period and in the official_rule.

REUNION AIRFARE - AVAILABLE ONLY TO UNACCOMPANIED SCHOLARS. Section 10.8.1 defines the reunion airfare as providing 'unaccompanied scholars with return travel to their home country for a reunion visit during institution semester breaks'. Section 10.8.3 disqualifies a scholar if any dependent family member accompanies them to Australia or joins them for an extended period, 10.8.5 requires twelve months unaccompanied in Australia and enrolment for a minimum of two academic years, and a change from unaccompanied to accompanied ends the entitlement permanently. Section 10.8.2 confirms eligibility 'will be confirmed in the letter of offer and contract', so it must be checked per scholar.

FIELDWORK RESTRICTED TO RESEARCH. Section 12.3 makes fieldwork available 'for research purposes only', in the form of one return economy airfare via the most direct route to the country of citizenship or within Australia. A bachelor's degree by coursework does not attract it, and 10.8.5 notes a scholar entitled to fieldwork may not claim a reunion airfare in the same year where the fieldwork is in the home country.

The Australia Awards Pacific Scholarships (Policy Handbook updated June 2023) fund study in the Pacific region rather than in Australia, and the Australia Awards Mekong-Australia Partnership, Australia Awards Maritime Security Scholarships, Australia Awards Brunei, Australia Awards Singapore, Australia Awards French Territories and the ACIAR John Allwright Fellowship are separate schemes with their own eligibility and processes that appear as separate options in the OASIS scheme drop-down.
